(1) hydrogen bond interactions between active site groups and the O3β atom of a nucleotide substrate are conserved in diverse phosphoryl transfer active sites; (2) these interactions are consistent with the hypothesis that they stabilize a transition state in which the scissile P-O bond is lengthened; (3) these interactions are also consistent with the hypothesis, derived from quantum mechanical calculations on small model compounds, that they stabilize the transition state by weakening the scissile O-P bond through

the active site configurations of diverse phosphoryl transfer enzymes are statistically similar and that this similarity is reflected in a pattern of hydrogen bonding interactions with the O3beta atom of the substrate phosphate that is conserved across enzyme families.

hydrogen bonding to the O3β atom of a nucleotide substrate is a common feature of many diverse phosphotransferases, and that this interaction may modulate the scissile P-O bond by altering the electronic structure of the phosphate group, as well as by affecting the electrostatic environment.
